summary: This humorous informational RFC comments on how hard it is to pick a distinctive hostname for your computer as the Internet grows. It is a light-hearted commentary rather than a technical specification, and was published on April 1.

eli5.summary: Everyone wants to name their pet something special, but so many pets exist that every good name is taken.

questions: how to name a computer host
subtitle: A humorous meditation on the challenge of naming computers

tldr.problem: As the Internet grows, finding a distinctive hostname for your computer becomes increasingly difficult because good names are already taken.
tldr.mechanism: This memo, formatted as humorous poetry, explains that every host needs three different names: a practical everyday name, a fancier optional name, and one special mystical name that only the nameserver knows.
tldr.outcome: The memo is a lighthearted commentary that plays on T.S. Eliot's poem about cats, not a technical specification. It was published on April 1st as a joke.

today: RFC 2100 remains an Informational RFC. It is a celebrated example of an April Fools day joke in the RFC series and is often cited as a humorous reflection on naming practices in the early Internet.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: This RFC is a humorous commentary on the difficulty of choosing a distinctive hostname for your computer. As the Internet grows exponentially, the problem becomes worse: more computers exist, fewer good names remain available. The memo is addressed to everyone except T.S. Eliot (author of the poem on which it is based) and David Addison (who dislikes a particular poetic meter).
sections.eli5: Picking a computer name is hard because the Internet is so big. This memo is a joke about that problem.

sections.title: The Three Names
sections.content: In poetic form, the memo explains that every host must have three distinct names. First, there is the practical everyday name, such as venus, athena, cisco, or sirius—sensible names that users work with daily. Second, there are fancier names chosen for elegance or specific purposes, such as mercury, phoenix, orion, or charon. Third, and most mysteriously, there is a peculiar name that no human research can discover: the name that only the nameserver knows and will "usually confess." This third name is described as ineffable, effable, and inscrutable.
sections.eli5: The poem says computers need an everyday name that people use, a fancier name if you like, and one secret name that the nameserver knows but nobody else does.

sections.title: Credits and References
sections.content: The memo acknowledges contributions from Don Libes, Mark Lottor, and creative system administrators who provided source material. It credits Andrew Lloyd-Webber and Cameron Mackintosh (the creators of the musical Cats) with inspiring the structure, and T.S. Eliot, whose poem "The Naming of Cats" provided the foundation. The memo references Don Libes' article on choosing computer names, a 1997 domain name survey, and a collection of cool hostnames on the web.
sections.eli5: The memo thanks people who gave examples and ideas, and it is based on a famous poem by T.S. Eliot about cats.
